blocks.x: Why don't you put your name on it first?
My name's Joseph Clark.
That's your full name, huh?
That's my full name.
And your name?
Charlotte Victor, V-I-C-T-O-R. I see.
Marjorie Zander.
Bill Russell.

And I'm Dick Allen. And let's see, we're recording this at 1717 Drive in the back in Clark's kitchen. And today's date is November? The 11th. November the 11th, 1959. Okay. Let's see. Where did we leave off? I believe you were talking about your teacher. You've been telling about the methods that Perkins used, too. I'd like to know a little bit more about that, how he taught you. Well, he, he, he, he, he, he, he, he, he, he, he, he, he, he, he, he, he, he, he, he, he,

he taught me the trombone. That's my voice instrument. And then later on, as I told you before, I switched to the bass. And I like the bass now. I don't think I'll play any other instrument now until I pass. I like all the instruments. So I like all the instruments. As I told you before, the instruments that we want, we can't get. That is the E flat clarinet, baritone, and the peck horn. No more of them. No more of them.
No more E flat clarinet.

No more. What about Paul Barnes? Well, Paul Barnes, you see, I heard of Paul Barnes, but I never did know him until he came into this band. And Paul Barnes is a nice musician, fine musician. He really is. But he's getting used to the band now.
And he's never played the E flat before?

No, he told us when he came, when we hired him, he says, fellas I don't have an E, I have a B. Well we tried the B, but you see the B don't fit in this band. You see, but it's all right. You see, they playing the high register. But now he told us that he was going to buy an E, and he bought the E. And you heard him the other day on that. So it fits like something similar to old time. But baritone and peck horn, Mr. Russell, goodbye no more. The youngsters of the day that's playing them instruments, why, they just got that bop stuff with them. You see what I mean? I listen to them school bands. That bop's what?
Bop.

Bop. We call it bop. Bop stuff. We call it bop stuff. See? They're not interested in this kind of music. They play those marches in the schools because they have to. And they play them so you hardly know what they're playing.
They have to run with them for one thing.

They run and all. That's why the organization, some of them hire those bands because they, you know, just give them whatever they want to give them. You see? And they take them. But you take like the organizations we work for, no school band. Uh-uh. Nope. No school band for that. Because I know across the river over there, there's a fella belongs to the young man and he said one day at the theater, he said, why don't you give, he said, my boy has got a, belongs to a band. He said, why don't you give my band, my boy's band a chance to play a funeral. He said, what band? He said, that band over there, a school band my son belongs to. He said, man, your son can't play no funeral across. No. No. Well, after these, this time came, when these bands came into the picture rather, all the old carnival parades had nothing else but ten piece bands. They didn't use nothing else but ten piece bands because I remember that myself. And later years when the parades got bigger and these schools set up these bands where these men belonged to these different organizations, they had their grandchildren and their nieces and nephews and all that and their sons and daughters in them bands while they give them, excuse me, they give them a break. But I know myself in the time when they just had the Moments Parade, Protus, Rex, and on a Monday you used to have, well the king came in, that was a big parade on a Monday. You used to have soldiers and sailors in that parade. That parade would be on a Monday about 12, 1 o'clock in the day. And that night was-
What king was that?

Rex came in the day before? Rex come in the day before, on a Monday. But now, in the later years when all these other Hormies and Babylon and all that come in the picture, they did away with it. In other words, they did away with that during World War II. World War II changed a lot of things, Mr. Russell. Just like the young men of liberty down there, they used music at every funeral. But when World War II broke out, after they asked not to have no crowds or nothing, assembly no crowds or nothing, that went out of the picture. And those parades didn't use anything but ten piece bands. And I notice now sometime on that Mormons parade, which is a Thursday night, there's a band, they call it the Reliance Band. I see it nine then, and all old men in that band. It makes me think back of old times, like things used to be. And I like things of old times. They say I'm old timey, but I know old timey is the best. I know that. This modern stuff is all right, fast and everything, but they're going to the cemetery a little faster than they should go. We're all going someday, but they're going a little faster than they should go. Everything's too fast. See? So those bands, I don't know. I don't know what it'll be later on.
Did you ever play any Mardi Gras parades yourself? You mean the big parades?
The big Mardi Gras. No, no, no, never did. Never until the night. Never did. Never did.
Well back to Perkins, I wanted to get some of the methods down that he, how would he tell
you to hold them? He played them. He played them. Oh yeah, he played them. He played in orchestras in the Roosevelt Hotel. He played them.
How would he let you hold your trombone? Did he have any instructions on that?
He had instructions to hold the trombone.
Use a method book?

Use a method. You hold the trombone in this finger between the first finger and the thumb. And you hold a slide between the two first and second finger and the thumb. Don't put your grasp it like that. You hold it with your two first finger. The tips of the finger. Just the tip of the finger and use the wrist, not the entire arm. The only time that you would stretch your arm if you make a note in the sixth position. But from the first position down to the fourth, you just use your wrist. Just let your arm be a couple inches from your body and use your wrist like a hinge on a door. That's the way he taught you. Because I know he used to tell Joe Harris all the time, don't draw your arm, you're not going to punch nobody.
Now how did that work with the placement on your lips? Where would you put your mouthpiece on your lips?
Just like you do now. Yeah, and you use that same system.
Use the same system. And keep this hand away from the body just like that.
Keep the left hand up. Keep the left hand up. Left elbow up. Left elbow up all the time. Well would you place, say, two thirds of the mouthpiece on your upper lip or one third or half?
One third.
One third. One third. One third on your upper lip. That's right.

One third. Then it would be two thirds on the bottom. That's right. And how do you produce the sound? Did he give you any particular sound? Well he always tells you when you go to make a note, he says don't blow in the instrument.

He says just like if you have something on the end of your tongue. He says that's what it is. He says you don't blow the instrument. Those fellow used to blow them and pump their jaws. He said that instrument wasn't made to make you ugly, that instrument was made to play. He says you just like you got something on the end of your tongue. And a note would come and I practiced that. I tried it a lot of times. And I do it now. Sometime if you've got a whole note, if you're playing a funeral march you've got a whole note, sometimes it takes you a little wind, you know, you strike it with your tongue first though. You always strike with your tongue.
Now, when you're holding a note like that, did he teach you anything on breathing, any special methods?
Well he said to take enough breath at the time, before you strike the note. To show and take enough breath.
Now what part of your mouth do you breathe from? Do you breathe through the horn or breathe from the side?
No, I breathe from the corner. You breathe from the corner. Yeah, when I take breath, I take breath from the corner. I take breath from the corner of my mouth. Did he teach you that?
He taught me that.
He taught me, see, never draw in from this one. Always take your breath from the corner of your mouth.
Do you remember the name of the method, who wrote the method that you used, the books?

The method that I was taught out of? The Perkins. Well, Arthur Langlands. I have one laying around here somewhere now that I bought with a bass. I don't know where it is. I'm familiar with that. But it's somewhere around here. My wife had all those things when she was living, she kept all those things in a certain spot. And it's around here in some of these boxes.
I wanted to ask a little bit more about Perkins. What was his main instrument when he took a job and played in bands? What?
Well his main instrument that I know was the bass.
The big tuba.
Yeah, he had a horn like mine but it was a four-valve bass. It had four valves. And it was an E flat.
Did you ever see him play drums any time?
Well no, no more than teaching the fellas around his house.
Or the trombone on Perkins?
The trombone, he had the trombone. He kept all those instruments that the scholars would like, they would come, he'd have all those instruments hanging on the side of the wall.
I wanted to ask about a studio. Where was that 6th Street?

That's, uh, Mr. Russell I really don't know, I really don't know the number of that house. But it's on 6th between Dryde and Barone on the uptown side of the street. And it's about the second house from Barone Street coming toward Dryde's.
We never got to know him of course so I was curious.
No, he passed, he passed oh long years ago. Let me see now. I really don't know exactly the year that he passed. What was he like?
I understand he was very light colored. He was, he was.
If you didn't know him you'd take him for white man. If you didn't know him.
Was he a friendly sort of fellow?
Friendly with everybody.
Was he very strict on his pupils?

Oh yeah, he was strict. If you went there, you see when you take a lesson and, uh, when you get through, you say, well we'll try this next week. He'll turn that page. He'll run two, three lines with you, say that'll be enough for you to practice. And he'll stay on that with you 10 or 15 minutes and give you an idea of it. All right, you go back next week and you don't make one note or don't do nothing with that lesson at all. He'll tell you, you have been practicing, go back home and come back next week. Now let me show you how that goes and he'll show you again.
Did he play it for you?

He played, when he taught you he picked up the trombone right side of you, the trumpet the same way, bass the same way. He had a little upright bass there. Little bit of thing, looked like a, looked almost like an upright alto. It was very small but it had good volume, one of them old timers, you know. And he'd pick that up, each scholar. The drums the same way.
What was the studio like? Was it in the front room or back?

No, it was in the back. It was in the back. It was between his bedroom and the kitchen. And they had like a, like a stairs to go up, upstairs. It had, well it wasn't no upstairs but it was a law. And they had a hole cut in the ceiling. And this thing was made something like a ladder. And he used to go up on that thing and that's where he had all those instruments up there. And all that old music and stuff he had up there.
Did he have a piano in the room?
No, he didn't have no piano, no.
Any music racks much or bench?

Oh yeah, he had plenty of music racks. Had plenty of music racks and chairs, a lot of chairs in there and all. And he used to be, he'd teach in that room. He taught us by oil lamps, no electric. But those lamps were the brightest day. Miss Perkins kept them that way. And he would set that lamp in front of you and put a card behind it to keep it from the light glaring you. And it would shine on the music. And he would always sit on your right and let you be on the left.
That's a very good picture of how they placed the lamp and how you studied it.
That's right. That's right.
Did he charge you a lot? Huh? Did he charge you a lot for our license?
Charge your dollar a lesson.
That's quite a bit in those days I bet. Charge your dollar a lesson.

When you sit down and he looked at his watch and he didn't stop and lose no other time when you're talking. He kept you on that instrument. Now when your time was up he'd pull his watch up and say, well your time is up but let me run over this with you.
How long did you usually run? An hour?

One hour. One hour. One hour. But I was smart though. I used to always go on Wednesday nights when there wouldn't be many scholars there. I'd get a little bit more. Because he used to like to talk to me about my father. He used to like to talk about, he said, Aaron was a fine man. He said, boy if you ever make the musician he was you'll be alright. He said, fine musician. He used to talk about him all the time. And I used to tell him all the time, I said, well first I didn't know him. I didn't want to see his picture. He said, you bring it around someday and let me see it. See what it looks like. So my mother was living then and I asked her about it. She says, what you want to do with it? I said, well, my music teacher, Mr. Perkins wants to see it. She says, now listen. I'm going to let you take this picture but I want you to bring it back tonight. He says, I will. And I went up there and I showed it to him and he looked at it and he said, yes that's Aaron. That's him up and down. I remember him when he was in that, well they were young at that time, you see. And he spoke of the old Onward band and the old Excelsior band and different things like that.
Well he played in the bands too at times. One more thing before I forget it. In teaching you to count, what did he do? Did he make you count with your foot or that?
Yes, he'd make you count with your foot. Make you count with your foot.
We got that on the other tape.
Yeah. I forgot about that. Yeah, he'd make you count with your foot. So I think I'll take that after I smoke. Okay.
Cough drop will get good. All right.
Let's see.
Who did you play your first job with?
First paying job or the first job?
First job of any kind. Of any kind?

Well I'll tell you, they set this concert band up, this fellow Pritchett. He set this band up. Well I had been practicing a lot and I'd been pinch hitting around with little bands all around, you know, different bands and all. So Willie Wilson, he was leading the record band at that time. And I knew Willie when he first came here. I knew him when he first came. He and Johnny. Willie worked at Sherwood's Pharmacy, which used to be at Canal and Durgin Wall. And Johnny, his brother, which was the baritone player, he was a butler for a family up in the Garden District around Coliseum and I think 8th or 7th in there somewhere, some of those people. Well anyway, they met me and they told me, he says, listen, he says, you know we're setting up a concert band, he says, why don't you come on down there and rehearse with us. I said, oh man, I can't play in no concert band. He said, you're not good enough. I said, listen, he says, you go to this number, there was three something south Rampart, Pritchett was then in the block, what they had a tailor shop in the block down there, Perdita, which is towed down now. Well I went down there and I saw him and I introduced myself to him and I told him who sent me. Well he got to talking with me and I told him, I said, well if that's how come, I said, but I don't think I'm good enough to play in. He said, that's what I want. He said, that's just what I want. He says, I want somebody like you that I can train to myself. I said, all right. So I thought the thing over, I said, well that might be a good chance for me to help them. Well they had rehearsing and went down to St. Catharines Hall then on La Salle near Tulane there, just over across from the charity hospital behind St. Catharines Church. Well I knew a lot of the fellas that was in that band, you know. So all of them told me, they said, man, this will help you. I said, this is what you ought to do. You ought to come. I said, well I'm going to try it anyway. So I went on there and set up those overtures and all I'd hit at them and miss and all that. So I felt kind of bad over it, you know. Some of them fellas said, man, I don't feel bad over that. This is your first time, man. I said, that's your first time. Well they kept on around there. So some of them fellas was taking the music, asking them to take the music home, you know. So I said, well I'm not going to ask them to take the music home. What I'm going to do, I'm going home and get my methods. And I'm going to get on those triplets and see what's to it. So I came home and I picked up the method. Practiced and that a lot. So this band set up and they rehearsed that band for about a year. And there was a fellow in Hot Springs, Arkansas by the name of John L. Webb. He had an outfit they called the Women of the Union. It was an organization. And he had sent bands, sent instruments all over to different people, different cities where he had these, this outfit and they set bands up. Well they got to talking about going to Hot Springs, going to Hot Springs, going to Hot Springs. Well everybody was enthused over going to Hot Springs. They were going to meet a band from Wichita Falls, going to meet a band from Dallas, going to meet a band from Fort Worth, going to meet a band from Hope, Arkansas, all over. Well they got this band together and they started having rehearsals twice a week. And I never will forget, there's an overture called Light Calvary, Operatic Mingle, and what was that other one now? Ex Tempo. It was the three overtures. Well they worked on those three and they got them down pretty good. So we went on to Hot Springs. We met different bands from all over. I had about seven or eight bands out there, concert bands. Well all those bands that night, they got up on the stage and they played their warm-up number and they played a couple of little overtures and then the last one was to be the one that to be judged by. Well we were the last band to go up. So when they said the band from New Orleans, the people began to clap. And we got up there and we played our two little overtures and then we played this Light Calvary. And that's the one that took it. But we had to work hard to get it down. But he had most all the instruments that he needed. He had baritones, altos, clarinet, saxophone, trombones, basses. He had three basses. He had a good set up. But I don't know, after them fellas came back, I don't know, they just got, don't care about us, you know, these fellas say I was, and then depression come along, you see. How big a band was that? That band was about thirty-five men. And what was the name of it again?
Tonic Triad.

I have the picture of some of it up there. The late Tonic Triad, not the original Tonic Triad. I have a picture of the late Tonic Triad. Well after the Depression, you know, those fellas, they didn't have no money, you know, no job or nothing. The man just lost all interest in music. So I was lucky because I had a job. I was very lucky. I had a job all during Depression. Very lucky. And I thank God Almighty for it. So he couldn't get those fellas together anymore, you know. So, all right, so now I'm going to go, I'll go to the record now. You want to stop the record? Cut that off, cut that off.
In the Tonic Triad?
Well, yes. Al C. Landry, Willie Paggio, Willie Wilson, Johnny Wilson.
Now what instruments did they play?

Johnny Wilson played baritone. Willie Wilson and Willie Paggio played trumpet. And Landry, did you name it? Al C. He trumpet. Al C. would die. Yeah, that's right. And Andrew Stevens played bass. Oscar Grammer played bass, which Oscar, they tell me he has a stroke now. I don't know, I haven't saw him in years, I don't know. And as I told you, Johnny Wilson was baritone. And a fellow by the name of William Eber, he was a Jamaican, he played baritone. And a fellow by the name of Jones, he played clarinet. And Oscar Henry, trombone, I played trombone there. A fellow by the name of Tom Steptoe, which is past, he played trombone. And let's see who else now. There's a lot of them in there that I didn't know very well, but those men that I called I knew very well. Now the drummers was Albert Francis, he was a snare drummer. And this fellow Peter Raphael, which is Lost One Limb, he was the bass drummer. Fine drummers, both of them, read like anything. And let me see, oh yeah, a fellow by the name of Gil, he played alto, which we called the ! And a lot of others that I didn't know very well. I just knew them by sight, you know.
Maybe if we stopped and got the picture, we could refresh your memory a little bit that way, would that help? There's a picture, hand in some place, do you know where it is?
Charlie. We can move this. Go, go, go there and get that picture hanging up over there. Tony, that's not the old Tony tried. What year? Oh, I don't know, this was a year. The hair that colored there.
Was it after depression?

Oh yes, this was after depression. Now, you see, this is Pritchett. On the extreme right standing. This is Professor Dalmers. That's the bass player. Bass drum. That's the one that didn't show up on this job and caused me to switch the bass. He's the bass. Now that's Willie Pazio. No.
Yeah. That's Landry. I mean Landry.
That's Landry rather. This is Willie Pazio.
That's Peter Rayfield.
Who's the trumpet player that's kneeling? You know him?
Yeah. Now let me get my pencil off on it. That fellow there. Oh, I don't know him. That's why I tell you there's something that I don't know.
Now this is, this fellow here is Loomis Hamilton. That's George Hamilton's son. This is Bell. Well let's back up. He's a baritone.
Who was George Hamilton?
George Hamilton is this fellow. He plays what?
He played bass. He played bass and Loomis Hamilton played trumpet. Trumpet, yeah.
Now the baritone. And this is Oscar Henry. And this is a Lopis boy. His daddy runs that Undertaker place down on Dumaine Street.
He's a trombone player?

Yeah, he's a trombone, but I think he gave it up. And that's me. And this is Albert Warner. Now this fellow's name is Parnaret. That's a clarinet player. Now this is Albert Francis, the one I told you about.
Yes.
See?
Snare drum.
And this is Peter Rayfield. He played the bass drum.
Who was that baritone player there?

Bell. He was crippling his right arm. He used to finger that horn with his left hand. He had an arm drawn up from one side. I don't know, he said he had to fall off a horse when he was a boy and it affected his arm and drew it up.
I know that fellow.
That's old man Barberang.
Is it though? Yeah.
It looked old then too, didn't it?
Yeah.
Were these fellas playing?

All those fellas just were standing around. Where was this taken, did you tell us? That's taken out there in where, out there in Jefferson where the old racetrack, old racetrack used to be. Not this new one they built, the old one they had. That's why I say it's years back.
You had three saxophones, four. Yeah. Two girls and two boys. They looked quite young.
Well that's those Grisby girls.
Are they related to Pritchard or are they?
No, he works in their father's tailor shop.
I know he said Grisby and Grisby.
Yeah that's right, well those are Grisby girls.
And these two boys? Well I don't know them.
See these fellas, I don't know those at all. I tell you a lot of them in there I don't know.
One boy may be playing a tenor and the other alto, I can't see too well. Where? Here, tenor saxophone and alto.
No, that's alto. Alto.
All four of them are alto saxophone? Alto, yeah.
That kid looks familiar to me. I don't know who that kid is. Fair enough.
He looks like a trumpet player, Red Russo.
He looks like Red Russo the trumpet player, that's funny.
Well Joe, I'm going to see you tomorrow, yeah? Alright, Charlie.
Alright fine, glad to meet you.
Bye.
Now, that was after depression, was it before World War II? What? Yeah, yeah, that's before World War II.
So it was somewhere in the 30s there, right? That's right. Well we'll check the date on that fair, we'll be able to find it.
And Patio took the picture, P-A-D-D-I-O, I guess. That's right, he suicided.
He did?
Yeah, he suicided from here along the bridge. Damn.
Did you have any relatives that anybody took over his photo studio or anything?
No one, no one, no one, no. They, after he suicided, I don't know what happened. He had a wife, I think, but nobody.
They probably threw all that stuff over him.
They took it, they'd gone away with him. God. He was a good photographer too, very good. He took it.
He took a nice picture.
It's a nice light, it shows up everybody's face by the way.
Yeah, it's dirty now, it needs to be cleaned.
Did you play in any dance bands while this was going on?
No.
You only played dance bands?
Never, never did play in no dance bands. Never did.
Never played string bass? No. Well what about this picture here? Did you play with any brass bands at that time, marching in the street?
No, not at that time. After this band broke up, then that's when I came into the Urica Band.
About what year was that?
Oh that's around 19, around 19 and 31, 32, one of those years.
Who was the other trombone when you joined?
When I joined? Well, Albert Warner.
Cornish wasn't anything?
Cornish had taken sick.
Alright. But whose place did you take?
I took Cornish's place.
Oh, I see.

I took Cornish's place. You see they had been using different trombones, I don't know, they were scouting around. So I went to their rehearsal one night. True, I knew all of them and they all knew me. And I sat down and rehearsed with them. So coming home, Ed Barrett, the bass player, and Will Wilson and Johnny Wilson, we walked.

Okay, we're going. We were walking home or something like that?
Mm-hmm. After this rehearsal?
Yeah, we walked home.
Well, that's ready.
Go ahead, I'm sorry.

Ready? And, uh, well, Red says to me, says to me, he says, you know they call me Red? He says, Red, you know what you ought to do? I said, what? He said, you spur up a little bit more, you come down to the hostel. I said, all right, Red, I will. Well, they kept on, kept on. So, I don't know, something happened and, well, they had a funeral. That's right. The first funeral I ever played. And it was for the young men on Olympia. I never will forget it. And that funeral we left used to meet then at 6 in Robertson. That's where the project is or not.
Want somebody to do it? Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
I was asking about the Elks Club since the Young Men Olympians use that. Is there any relation there? Do they just rent it or what?

No. They just rent that place. You see I belong to Young Men Olympians and we pay two and a half a meeting. We meet twice a month. We meet the second and the fourth Sunday of each month. But that building belongs to the Elks.
That's the one that was the Bulls Club.

It used to be the Bulls Club years ago. And they went to the Wall. Well the Elks bought it. And as I was saying, the Young and True Friends were there in Carlton and the Eagles and they were there. Well I played for the Eagles occasionally. And I played for the merry-go-rounds
occasionally. What is the Eagles?
Well that's the one up there in Carlton too but they meet somewhere around in there, around Hoist Street. Around Hoist and the Chil-
Is that near Adams and Dominican?
Yeah, below that though. Two blocks below. Around Cherokee they meet around in there.
Who's the Grand Marshal? Louis Handy? Is that the guy?
Yeah, Louis Handy is the Grand Marshal for the Eagles.

The Eagles, did they ever have a clubhouse on Eagle Street? There was one years ago I remember in an old directory. I wondered if the organization got their name from the Eagle Street No. All over the country. All over the country there's an Eagles organization too I know. That Eagle. Sorry, don't worry about that. We all got a call.

They are. No, they're smoking. This Eagles set up in the later years. See this Eagles set up in the later years. I remember when they set it up because I played for dedication at Bantam. Were they on Eagle Street at that time? No. They're right where they are now. They meet in that hall at Adam and Dominican. That's where they meet at. They always did meet there. And the President belongs to the young men of Olympia also. Most of the men, a lot of the men belongs to the Eagle and the Olympia and the young and true friends, you see, and they all belong to the same thing.
What about the young men, Olympians, the junior branch? That's related to the older ones?
Old men. They set up under that. They set up under us.
When the fellow gets older?
I was in the juniors when I was a boy.
So the one, do they go from one to the other when they get older?

Well you can. You can't switch. You see, I was in the junior when I was a boy. I was a boy about seven years old. And I stayed in that thing, I don't know, I guess I was about 13 to 14 years old and I got out. Then I went to Chicago and I stayed in Chicago for about six years. And when I came back, well I wanted to get back in, so I said, well I ain't going back in. The kids, we call them the kids. And I went on to the old men. And I've been in the old men ever since.
Any organizations downtown that have funerals or parades?

Well not anymore. See, years ago, Young Men of Liberty used to use music. Perseverance used music. The charity used music. And there was another organization down there, Young Men's by Dave. But you see, Dick, in the later years, old men die out. That's it. The youngsters don't come behind. They just fade out the pictures. They die out. That's the end of it. They used to have big parades on Sunday when those organizations were in bloom. Downtown and uptown. Downtown and uptown also. That's right. They used to have big parades. On a Sunday, what they call the anniversary parade. Start around nine in the morning, last until four or five in the evening. But no more of that because those organizations are all gone.
Well, the organizations mostly smaller than they used to be now or about the same size?

Oh, they were big. They had a lot of men belong to them. Yeah, they were very large. Fairlory. I remember when I was a boy, I guess in my middle teens, the art fellas, that's why I tell these art fellas that meet next door here to me, the older fellas like Green and Kemp Jackson and Allen Williams, all them old fellas that was long. You see, my uncle was an art fellow when I was a boy. My uncle belonged to number seven. And as I told you before, they have, they used to have 10th of May where they out. They had a parade in the day. They had a big picnic at the fairground that night. It would last all night long. You couldn't get through Padilla Street on the morning that parade was making up. Fellas with horses and wagons would want to pass. They'd have to go around Ramport or go around Saratoga. They couldn't pass in that block. It was just like carnival around there. They couldn't get enough bands. And I look at the art fellas today with what little handful they got. I can't believe it's art fellas. That's true. They had lodges all around Donaldsonville. All them lodges used to come here for that day, the 10th of May, which was a big day, but no more. And just like I tell Green and them now, I say, Green, you can say what you want. When you go, Kemp go, Allen go, Willie Williams, when you fellas go, goodbye art fellas from New Orleans, no more. Uh-uh. The younger man don't want to step in. Now, the art fellas we played for on the second Sunday thing. And you know, you know, you're going to be in the middle of the summer. And you're going to see the same faces every year when you go. So I asked an old man up there about these young men. He says, what did I tell you? He said, you know, these boys were born and raised here in the country. And they got to following their father's steps, grandfather, uncle, and all that. He said, they get in there and they stay in there. They don't get in there and get out. They stay in there. And I guess they stay in there and they'll grow old in there. Maybe their children don't take the steps. But, uh, I don't know. The fella here in the Orleans, he don't want that. Now you say the Jolly Bunch or something like that, why he's just wild for that. For one day only. I bet you right now they ain't 20 men financially in the Jolly Bunch. They had the parade, I believe, in July, wasn't it? Yeah, usually in August or July. August or July. I bet you they ain't 20 men in there financial. Bet you right now. But when that parade starts, that's where they all get in.
I noticed there was a pretty big group in the parade on Saturday. It looked like there were a number of young men in that group.
Where, Saturday up there? Oh, in Shrewsbury. Yeah, well, there's a lot of young men belong there. There's a lot of young men belong there.
There seem to be a lot of country people move in there or something.
Well, yes.
More in that style.
Yeah, that's right. That's right.

What's that one that's down below that you play for every year, down below the Industrial Canal? Industrial Canal. You know the church, where we go to church? The Masons, I think. The Sheik. Yes, indeed. She handles that fight. Usually handles it. They're belong students. Not funerals, but a Sunday. Dedication. A dedication it was on here. It's a parade. I think I missed it this year. Cornerstone Lane, I usually call it.
Well, you know, I'll tell you. There's no organizations down there, but you see, sometimes the organizations have an occasion to go down there to lay a stone.
They go to a church on Maurice Street. Chate Mall.
Yeah, well, we laid that cornerstone and then the Oddfellas had their memorial service there in May.
Those are Oddfellas too then?
That's the Oddfellas, yeah. These are Oddfellas that meet next door here. That's the ones. Yeah.
But who has Memorial Day in Chalamet?
Oh, that's the 30th of May.
Which organization is that?
Well, that's set up by what they call the American Legion Handlers, now I think.
Oh, yeah.

I'm not sure. Because you see, I really don't know because the union sends us there on that day. And all we do is get the man that's sponsoring that thing to sign the paper. We don't know who's ahead of it, who's giving it. We just go down there and work and get him to sign that paper and that's it. We don't know who's who down there. But years ago, when they used to go down there and they used to go down there and stay all day, they would have speaking and they have singing and they would have baskets and they'd sit out and they'd spend the day down there. Well, they used to have what they used to call that Grand Army Day. That's the War of 1861, I think. I think they used to, yeah.
Grand Army of the Republic.

That's right. They used to call that Grand Army Day down there. But it's the same thing now, but it's changed over because all those, a lot of those old soldiers living at that time. Excuse me, but a lot of them is gone now. Yeah. See, most all of them are gone. So these younger fellas from these other wars, like World War I and World War II, they're supposed to take it over, but I don't know. They don't gather like they used to. A few go down, you know. The old timers, they go down. They speak of the old times, but not like it used to be.
What about the Masons? Do you all ever play for them?
Yeah, we play for them.
For what kind of things?

Well, you see, years ago, the Masons used to use music at every funeral. But I don't know, in the later years, these men that come into these things, they kind of abolish that. But that's in the Constitution. Every Mason is supposed to be buried with a band of music. But these fellas get away from it, some kind of way, I don't know. See what I mean? Some of them say the bands is too high and all that. The bands are not too high because they're not paying much of members pay for it.

So what about a Mason who's a Catholic? Can he... No, Masons can't be Catholics. No, Catholics can't be Masons. Are you sure? I'm pretty sure. Is that right? That's what I hear. Yeah, that's what I've always heard and I'm sure. Yeah, but I've seen it happen here. Maybe. I've seen it happen in New Orleans. Yeah. It could be. That's why I'm asking. Because I can point out something to you later. Okay.
Well, things have changed in the later years. Things are not like they used to be.
But what about Catholics? Did you ever bury Catholics with music yourself?
No.
You never have. No.
So you don't know how long ago it was that the church said that they couldn't be buried with music?
Huh?
Apparently some people remember having played for Catholic funerals.
Well, I don't remember. I've been to Catholic cemeteries though.
Are you a Catholic?
I am.
You are a Catholic?
I am.
There's some rule from the Archbishop on that and I never have been able to...
Now, I don't know. I've never played a Catholic funeral. But we have, we have went to a Catholic cemetery with a body.
With the band.
With the band. But the band don't go in the cemetery.
No.

I don't know. You see that St. Mary's cemetery up on Red Street there from the Young Men's Hall as we'd been going up? Yeah. That's a Catholic cemetery. I've been there two, three times with bodies but never go in.
Did you meet the funeral at the home or under the father?

No, we meet at the church like we always did. At the church. That's right. Catholic church. Now that man, I think those people, I think they have tombs of their own in there. They bury in there. Like Peter Bocard, they have a tomb in there. A family tomb. And the funerals we take there, I think those people have family tombs in there. I think that's the way that thing works.
Well, what other religions do you play for?
Well, mostly Baptist. Methodist sometimes.
But do you ever play for anything else besides Baptist and Methodist?
No.
No spiritualist or elements or anything like that? No.

Well, years ago, there used to be a spiritualist church back here on Mel Palmer, the street. And that lady died. She used to have a parade every year. And they used to all come out barefoot, no shoes on, hot broad and sun. Everybody be barefoot. Everybody but the band. And they'd walk in that hot sun barefoot and have on their white gowns and things like that. But she died. They don't have it. And I don't know if that church is there anymore. They used to call her Mother Kate.
Did they have funerals too?
Oh no. They'd have funerals at that church if someone passed. But not with a band? No, no, no band. No.
Have you ever played for a woman?
Yeah, occasionally. Occasionally.
Would they be religious leaders or would they be members of an organization?
What, the women?
The women in the funeral, you know.
Well, you see, you take these women that hold these high orders in the Eastern Star, cultural ampers, and all the big high positions in there where they give them music. Sure.
I've never seen one. I've never seen one.
I've played them. I've played them many times.
In late years? Yeah.
I think so. I think so.
Mm-hmm.
Was there any difference in what you'd play for a woman or anything? No, same thing. Same thing. Same thing.
Same thing.
Coming back, you'd play the same thing?
Mm-hmm. Coming back the same way. Yeah. That's the way it goes.
Well, you tell me something about, you mentioned Dick did something about a sample. Did you all ever give samples of how did that work?

Percy was telling me about how Buddy Petit and his brother Earl Humphrey would go around and give a sample for the wood at the quake. Have you ever heard of that? No. Well, that sounds like Buddy Petit. No, that's a joke. Percy was just joking. That's a joke. We got to see him and ask him about it.
That's a joke, Dick.
That's the trouble. You get things down as history and then you go and ask somebody else and take it down.
That's right.
Which is why you gotta check him. That's a joke.
That's a joke.
Well, you all, if we could sort of start a funeral, you meet where usually to start? Where the band meets. Where the organization meets.

See, some of them meet different places. See, like over there they meet, over there, that hall over there, like up here they meet up there. Wherever they meet, they disband, they go and make a human disband in the same place. Would it always be a hall? Well, mostly, yeah.
Do you ever meet at a person's home?

No, no, never do. No. Now the only way you meet at a person's home is if a fellow passes and don't belong to anything that uses music and the boys get together and scrape up money to hire a band, they say, well, meet us on City City Corner. You see, they'll meet on some corner somewhere and then they'll go to this home or this church or wherever this body is and they'll go, come back and they'll break up on that same corner. That's the only way that people, most of all the organizations, they got some kind of a hall to meet. That's right. Yeah.
Well, on Saturday when you all went, when the body was in the home instead of in the church, is that usual or is that?

Well, no. No. See, most of the time those bodies be in the Undertaker Parlor or at a church, but you see, this fellow didn't belong to any church, you see. That's why they didn't go to no church with them. They had their service in their home. See, that's how that was. But very seldom you get one like that, very seldom. It's either at the Undertaker Parlor you meet them or either at the church.

Well, as to whether you meet them at the Undertaker Parlor or the, do you ever meet them there and then take them to the church? That's right. Yeah. Well, would that sort of depend on how far the distance was as to where you meet them?
No, it don't depend on the distance at all. The distance don't have anything to do with it. That's right. The distance don't have anything to do with it.
Why would they be laid out in that church?

Well, you see, sometimes the family wants their body wake in the church at night. See, when you find those bodies at those churches, they've been in there all night. See, they have a wake like tonight and when the wake is over, they close the church up and the next day they go there and they open up and they have a service. Most of the time it's like that.
Most of the time the body's all in the church.

Oh yeah, in Algiers, yeah, you know, get a body out of a hall or out of a house or Undertaker Parlor very seldom, very seldom you get a body out of an Undertaker or a home over there, always in the church.
I never knew that, in Algiers.

That's right. Very seldom. It's always at one of those churches or they are either at the Undertaker, but I, very seldom. I've played quite a few from Henderson's, but most of my few was from the church, most of them.
I'm wondering, change the subject a little, what was the biggest funeral you ever played with more bands, most bands and all? Well, I'll tell you, this Undertaker,

the Murray Henderson, he had five bands. That's what Kid Thomas told me the other day too. Five bands and the next one was old man Allen, he had four bands. I played both of those films. I just had to come into the Urica Band at that time. We had a bass player at that time by the name of Joe Howard. You heard of him? Used to be a trumpet player, but he paralyzed his lip when he went to bass. He paralyzed the nerve of his lip. He was making those high notes all the time, just just paralyzed his lip. He could play a nice bass player though. He made a nice bass player.
Well, how long has it been since you've played a funeral with more than one band?
Oh, it's been quite a while. A lot of this about a year or so. I believe you was on that last one when John Cashman was with us. I remember you had two bands. That's it. That's the last one I played.
How many did Celestan's funeral have? Three or?
Well, let me see. They had us, they had John,

and I think. Two fifteen men bands. That was the way it was. That's the way it was. But it was just two. Yeah, two or two. Thirty men in all. That's all. And they just added on to the band. That's right. That's right. Do you remember Buddy Petit's funeral?
I played it.
How many bands were there?
One.
Just one? I thought it was a great big...
No.
You think of Kid Renee's? No. No.

They scrapped up a band for that funeral. Kid Howard scrapped up he and Ernest Rogers. Oh, right. And they went to a church down on Annette Street somewhere. And was it Annette? I think it was Annette. Annette or Lapa Roof somewhere. One of those streets downtown I know. Because Ernest called, come to me and asked me, would I go? I said, yeah, I'll go. By being a musician, you know, we all volunteered and went. And he had a nice funeral. Nice funeral.
Is he a Catholic?
No. They're taking him to the Baptist Church, I think it was.
Well, when you have more than one band, do they play right after each other? I mean, or...
Yeah. That's the way we do. We play one and they play one.
But you all are lined up right after each other. No, different spots. Well, that would be when more than one organization was mentioned. That's right. That's right. I see.
The different organizations hire different bands. Let me say, guys, remember two organizations, each one can hire a band?
Yeah.
Well, can one organization hire two bands?
No. No. They don't do it.
Well, how do you line up then? The Grand Marshal comes first, huh?
That's right.
In one organization. And then the... Which Grand Marshal? Which Grand... Well, I'll say...
Well, the one that has the body in charge. The organization that has the body in charge always goes first. And the other organizations go behind.
What do they go behind, though?
I mean, they drop back in the back. They go second.
Is the first in between or... No.
On the tail end, all the way. The two organizations always in front.
Well, how do you decide which organization has the body in charge?

Well, I don't know how they run that, you see. That's kind of complicated to me. When I go there and I bring my band to where I'm going to work. Well, they go there and then when they come out, say, well, we got this body in charge, we're going to leave. Sometimes they say, well, they're going to take it. And then we're going to take it. And then we're going to take it. It's like that funeral we got ahead over there last year sometime. Over the Vidoc down there around Wagner Street. I don't know if you remember that, Mr. Russell. I believe he was on that funeral. It was on a Saturday. And they had two bands over there. So Clitto, that's Marshall for the young men, he said, well, they got the body in charge, they're going to leave. So they led. They did. It was all right. I like them to lead sometimes.

What, back to going from the hall or wherever you meet the corner to the pick up the body, what kind of music would you play before you get to where the body is? Play hymns. Only hymns. That's right. Yeah. Nothing. But then fast tempo. That's right. Fast march. It should take time. Yeah. So you're with the body. You've picked up the body, either the church or the home or the undertaker, wherever it was. What would you play then?
What, leaving that?
With the body.
Oh, you'll have to play a funeral march. Or one of those manuscripts. Just like we do all the time.
I want to get it down on tape. I know.
What tempo? Slow. Four-four time?
Mm-hmm. Real slow.
Slow, yeah.
And then in the cemetery?
Well, they always play a number from the march or to the grave, you see, we play some kind of slow number on the march to the grave.
Do you all decide that or do they ever ask you to play certain things?
Well, sometimes they come and request, give you a request on sentences to him. Sometimes they don't rule, we play what we want.
Has anybody ever requested something real unusual or anything like that?

Well, I tell you, now and then you get somebody asked for Nero My God to the grave. And we haven't played that in so long. You know what I mean? All the bands used to play that time, they'd bring a body out the house, Nero My God to the grave. You see? And it's just, that's the, I mean, not that they're against the hymn, no. But it's just constantly all the time. I remember I went to Carlton to play a fume one day, and I was surprised that the young and true friends had hired me. And we got up there and some of the members said, well, we will hear something different today. So I was wondering what happened. Now I didn't say nothing, you know. So when I went to pray the fume. Come on, got to the hall. So when he came out, you know, you see, you didn't hear the same thing you been hearing all along. Well, I didn't say anything, you see, because I don't want them fellas to think that I'm trying to hammer on them or nothing like that, you know. But I know what he meant, you see, but I never did say nothing. But I always try to play something different when I go to a job. You see, to try to change around. You can change around. I got enough there to change around. Yeah, sure. See what I mean? But some fellas, I don't know, they got them bands that go and they play the same thing all the time. What a friend we have in Jesus. Near my God to thee.
Closer walk is what I'm around.

That's right. We don't play that no more. I told the fellas, leave that on the side. Don't play it no more. Let it rest. And do Mr. Russell not to brag, but do you know we the first band to play that on the street? You were. That's right. We had Louis de Mille to write that thing for us. It's somewhere in one of these boxes. I don't know what's in there or in one of them other boxes. We the first band to play that on the street.
How many boxes do you have?
I got another one up there somewhere.
I think you must have a dozen. You're not telling us about them.
I don't have a dozen. I don't have a dozen.
You got quite a few though.
I got quite a few. I got enough to take care of it all right.
Well about how many funerals do you suppose you've played through the years?
Through my years? Well I don't know. That's a hard problem. That's a hard problem.
Would you say one or two a month or one a week?

A month? I saw myself when I played winning the record man. I played one every day. Or one solid week. I'll never forget that. Fellas would say man, they'd say man, man the way they passed in there, woo woo. We would get the shake out ourselves. One a day. I played three in a week. I have played two in a day. I played one ten in the morning and one morning in the evening. Two in the evening rather. That's right. That's Willie Pichaud. He'll tell you. But to say how many I played during my musical career, that's a hard problem. But I know it's over five hundred. I know that.
What about now? How many do you play a month now you say?
Well I don't know Dick. I'll have to. All right. You do keep it down. You've got to go down. Turn it off. Oh that's all right. Leave it on. I'll leave it.
Turn it off for a minute Phil.
18, 19, 20 this year.
20. What about January? Nothing in January?
No.
You didn't have a single parade or a single funeral? No.
No.
And this is the middle of November so that's...
And that's last year?
Almost two a month.

That's last year. It looks about the same. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen. That's last year. It's 56. This is the year right after she died. That's one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve. Twelve and it all rests in the parade.
One a month. Thirteen. You skipped that one. Yeah.
Yeah.
Because John Kazimer has about as many funerals as your band too, doesn't he?
Well, I really don't know Mr. Russell. It's a hard thing to say. It's a hard thing to say.
So there's still two or three a month I think. Yeah. And then George Williams never does play any, huh?
Well, you see, I'll tell you. I don't know, but George, George don't care much about playing funeral.
Oh, I see.
He don't care much about it.

We better wind it up, haven't we? Yeah, I think there's about ten seconds left. Okay. Well, thank you a million. We sure do appreciate it. I enjoyed hearing about all those old times and the Eureka band too. Yeah. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Thank you.
